reading.delprov: Delprov B1a: reading – What Did They Say?
reading.title: What Did They Say?

image.alt: Two young people talking to each other.

reading.ingress: Two people are talking to each other. Read each dialogue. How does it end? Choose the best alternative.

paragraphs: In this part you read twelve short dialogues. Each dialogue has three lines. Your job is to choose the line that fits best as the fourth and last line.
Look at the example below.

Example:
– I went shopping yesterday.
– What did you buy?
– A pair of new shoes.
→ How much were they?
Read the whole dialogue and all four alternatives before you choose. Only one alternative is correct.

byline: I de nationella provens format – allt innehåll är nyskrivet.

questions.prompt:
– I've made pancakes.
– They smell great!
– Would you like one?
questions.explanation: Den tredje repliken är ett erbjudande, så det som passar är att tacka ja. Att säga att man inte tycker om pannkakor motsäger att man nyss sagt att de luktar gott.

questions.prompt:
– Have you seen my keys?
– No, where did you put them?
– If I knew that, I wouldn't be looking.
questions.explanation: Den sista repliken är ett vänligt påpekande om att frågan var onödig. Då är det naturligt att be om ursäkt för frågan. Att svara var nycklarna är går inte, eftersom personen just sagt att hen inte vet.

questions.prompt:
– Do you want to come to the cinema tonight?
– What film is it?
– The new one about the dragon.
questions.explanation: Personen som fick frågan svarar sist, och det enda alternativ som svarar på inbjudan är att man redan har sett filmen. Tiden för filmen skulle den som bjuder in ha sagt.

questions.prompt:
– You're late again.
– I'm sorry. The bus didn't come.
– That's the third time this week.
questions.explanation: Efter en tillsägelse passar det att lova bättring. Att säga ”I'm never late” motsäger det som just sagts om tre gånger på en vecka.

questions.prompt:
– Can I borrow your pen?
– Sure, here you are.
– Thanks, I'll give it back after class.
questions.explanation: Pennan är redan utlånad, så svaret ska vara vänligt och avslutande. ”I need it now” och ”I don't have a pen” motsäger att personen nyss lånade ut den.

questions.prompt:
– What are you reading?
– A book about volcanoes.
– Is it any good?
options: Yes, I can't put it down.
questions.explanation: Frågan gäller om boken är bra. Uttrycket ”I can't put it down” betyder att boken är så spännande att man inte kan sluta läsa. Priset svarar inte på frågan.

questions.prompt:
– My computer isn't working.
– Have you tried turning it off and on?
– Of course I have.
options: I'll buy you a new one.
questions.explanation: Personen har redan provat det enda tipset, så det naturliga är att erkänna att man inte har fler idéer. Att föreslå samma sak igen vore konstigt.

questions.prompt:
– We're going camping this weekend.
– Really? Where?
– By the lake, if the weather is good.
options: You can swim in the sea.
questions.explanation: Orden ”if the weather is good” gör vädret till samtalets ämne, och då passar en förhoppning om uppehåll. Alternativet om måndag motsäger ”this weekend”.

questions.prompt:
– Did you finish your homework?
– Almost. I've got one page left.
– You'd better hurry.
questions.explanation: Eleven har redan sagt att en sida återstår, så svaret måste stämma med det. ”I haven't started” och ”There's no homework” motsäger den tidigare repliken.

questions.prompt:
– This bag is really heavy.
– Do you want me to carry it?
– Would you mind?
questions.explanation: ”Would you mind?” är ett artigt sätt att tacka ja till hjälp, och det vanliga svaret är ”Not at all”, alltså ”inte alls, det gör jag gärna”.

questions.prompt:
– I'm going to the shop. Do you need anything?
– Could you get some milk?
– Sure. Anything else?
questions.explanation: Frågan ”Anything else?” ska besvaras med om något mer behövs. Att säga att man inte dricker mjölk motsäger att man nyss bad om mjölk.

questions.prompt:

questions.explanation: Eftersom det verkar bli regn är det logiska att föreslå ett paraply. ”The sun is hot” motsäger att himlen är full av moln.

reading.delprov: Delprov B1b: reading – Visit Brackenhill Farm Park!
reading.title: Visit Brackenhill Farm Park!

image.alt: A farm with animals in a green field.

reading.ingress: Use the information in the text when you answer the questions. Your answers must be in English.

paragraphs: Muddy boots, warm eggs straight from the nest and a goat that eats your shoelaces – Brackenhill Farm Park is a working farm where visitors are allowed to join in.

sections.heading: Where we are
paragraphs: Brackenhill Farm Park lies in the south-west of England, about ten miles from the city of Exford. The farm has been in the Brackenhill family for more than a hundred years and still keeps sheep, cows, goats, hens and two very old donkeys.

sections.heading: Opening times
paragraphs: The park is open every day from March to October. In winter we open at weekends only. Our gates open at 10 a.m. all year. We close at 5 p.m. from April to September, and at 4 p.m. in March and October.
Tickets cost £9 for adults and £6 for children under 15. Children under three come in free.

sections.heading: Become a Junior Farmer
paragraphs: At the gate you can pick up a free Junior Farmer booklet. The booklet is for children between 5 and 11 years old. Complete four or more activities and you will get a badge and a certificate with your name on it.
You can choose from many activities: feed the goats, collect eggs in the hen house, plant a sunflower seed to take home, or learn to milk our wooden practice cow.

sections.heading: What to see and do
paragraphs: Most of our barns have a roof, so a rainy day is never a problem. That is one reason why so many schools choose Brackenhill for their class trips – the other is that our animals are used to children and can be touched.
Along the main path you will find a farm shop with cheese and jam made here, a café with home-made cakes, and a small Tractor Museum. The museum is open every day and costs nothing to visit.
Outside the farm buildings there is a two-mile walking trail through our fields and a large wooden playground next to the car park.

sections.heading: Getting here
paragraphs: The number 14 bus stops at the farm gate, but it only runs twice a day. Most families therefore come by car, and parking is free. If you cycle, you can leave your bike in the shed by the entrance.

sections.heading: Before you come
paragraphs: Book your ticket online before you travel. At weekends and in the school holidays the park is often full by lunchtime, and we cannot let more visitors in.
Finally, remember that this is a real farm. Wear boots or old shoes – the fields are muddy even in summer.

reading.delprov: Delprov B1c: reading – The Ice Cream Queen
reading.title: The Ice Cream Queen

image.alt: An ice cream cart in a sunny street.

reading.ingress: This is a story about a woman called Ellen Brooks. Read the text and answer the questions after each part. Remember – your answers must be in English! When you answer questions with alternatives, choose one alternative only.

paragraphs: Ellen Brooks was born in 1934 in a small fishing town on the east coast of Scotland. Her father was a fisherman and her mother sold vegetables at the market. Ellen was the youngest of seven children, and the family had very little money.

When Ellen was nine, her father hurt his back and could no longer go out with the boats. From that day the children had to help. Ellen's job was to stand by her mother's table at the market every Saturday morning, calling out the prices so loudly that people three streets away could hear her.
She hated the cold. She did not hate the market. What she loved was watching people stop, smile and change their minds because of something she had said.

In the summer of 1952, when Ellen was eighteen, an Italian family opened a café in the town and began selling ice cream. Ellen had never tasted it before. She spent a whole week's wages on one cone, and she thought about it for years afterwards.

She wanted to sell ice cream herself, but she had no money for a shop. Instead she bought an old bicycle, took off the back wheel and asked the town's blacksmith to build a small cart in its place. It took her three months to save enough to pay him. She painted the cart yellow and wrote one word on the side: ELLEN'S.

The first summer was hard. She had no freezer, so she could only make as much ice cream as she could sell in a day, and on rainy days she sold nothing at all. Twice she thought about giving up. What stopped her was a promise she had made to her mother: she would try for three summers before she decided.

By the third summer people were waiting at the harbour before she arrived. Ellen had learned something the café owners had not: she asked her customers what they wanted. When children said the cones were too big, she made a smaller one for half the price. When fishermen came off the boats at five in the morning, she started coming at five too, with coffee as well as ice cream.

In 1961 she finally opened a shop. By 1975 there were fourteen of them along the coast, and newspapers had started calling her the Ice Cream Queen. Ellen never liked the name. ‘A queen sits down,' she said in one interview. ‘I have never sat down in my life.'

Ellen sold the company in 1989. She gave most of the money to a fund that pays for young people from her town to train for a job – a plumber, a cook, a nurse, anything they choose. When she died in 2019, at the age of 85, more than four hundred people came to say goodbye. Many of them had never met her. They had simply grown up eating her ice cream, or learning a trade with her money.

reading.delprov: Delprov B1b: reading – Pinewood Summer Camp
reading.title: Pinewood Summer Camp
reading.ingress: Use the information in the text when you answer the questions. Your answers must be in English.

paragraphs: Two weeks without a screen, a lake you can jump into before breakfast and forty new people who did not know your name on Monday. Welcome to Pinewood.

sections.heading: Where we are
paragraphs: Pinewood Summer Camp lies in the forest by Lake Ammer in southern Germany, an hour and a half by train from Munich. The camp has been open every summer since 1968.

sections.heading: Who can come
paragraphs: Our camps are for young people between 11 and 16. Each group has a maximum of twenty campers and four leaders, and we always keep boys and girls in separate sleeping cabins.
You do not need to speak perfect English. Our leaders come from six different countries and English is the language we all share.

sections.heading: When and how much
paragraphs: There are three camps every summer: one in late June, one in July and one in the first two weeks of August. Each camp lasts fourteen days.
The price is 690 euros. This covers your bed, all meals, all activities and the train ticket from Munich. It does not cover your travel to Munich, which you arrange yourself.

sections.heading: A normal day
paragraphs: We wake up at seven and swim in the lake before breakfast – this is not compulsory, but almost everybody does it after the first few days. Mornings are for activities you choose yourself: canoeing, climbing, photography, cooking or football.

Afternoons are quieter. Many campers read, play cards or sleep. At eight in the evening we meet at the fire, and every camper has to tell a story once during the two weeks. Some people dread it. Nobody has ever regretted it.

sections.heading: Rules
paragraphs: Phones are collected on the first evening and given back on the last day. We know this sounds hard, and we know from twenty years of doing it that after three days nobody asks for them.
The lake may only be used when a leader is on the beach. This is the one rule we never bend, and campers who break it are sent home.

sections.heading: Getting here
paragraphs: A camp bus meets every train at Ammersee station between two and six o'clock on the first day. If your train arrives later, write to us in advance and we will pick you up by car.
Bring a sleeping bag, a raincoat and shoes you do not mind ruining. Everything else you need is here.

reading.ingress: This is a story about a woman called Ines Halvorsen. Read the text and answer the questions after each part. Remember – your answers must be in English! When you answer questions with alternatives, choose one alternative only.

paragraphs: Ines Halvorsen was born in 1972 in Tromsø, a town in the far north of Norway where the sun does not rise at all for two months every winter. Her mother was a nurse and her father repaired radios in a small shop under their flat.

As a child Ines spent hours in that shop. She was not interested in the radios themselves. She was interested in the moment when her father finally got one working and a voice came out of it – a voice from Moscow, or London, or a fishing boat somewhere out at sea.

When she was eleven her father gave her a broken tape recorder and told her she could keep it if she could mend it. It took her a month. The first thing she recorded was the sound of the rain on the shop window.
Ines studied to become a sound engineer and got a job at a radio station in Oslo. For nine years she recorded interviews, concerts and adverts. She was good at it, and she was bored.

The change came in 2004, on a holiday in her old home town. She walked down to the harbour where the fishing boats had always been and found it almost empty. The boats were gone, and so were the sounds she remembered: the engines, the shouting, the ice being poured into the boxes.
She realised that nobody had ever recorded any of it. Photographs of the harbour existed in every museum in the north. Not one second of sound did.
That autumn she left her job. Her colleagues thought she was making a mistake, and for the first two years she earned almost nothing.

Since then Ines has recorded more than four thousand sounds in eleven countries. She records places that are changing or disappearing: a glacier melting, the last working paper mill in a valley, a school in a village where only nine children are left.

Her rule is that she never adds anything afterwards and never removes a sound she does not like. ‘If a car goes past while I am recording a bird, the car stays,' she says. ‘That is what the place sounds like. I am not making music.'

The recordings are free for anyone to listen to on a website she pays for herself. Schools use them, film-makers use them, and once a man in Canada wrote to say he had found a recording of a street in the town where he grew up, and had played it to his mother, who was ninety-one and had not been back for seventy years.
Ines keeps that letter on the wall above her desk. When people ask her why she does this work, she does not answer. She points at the wall.

reading.ingress: You're going to read a story about a girl, Nadia, and what happened to her one evening. Answer the questions after each part of the story. Your answers must be in English. When answering questions with alternatives – choose ONE alternative only.

paragraphs: It was a warm evening in early September. Nadia had been at a football match in Kirkby with her cousin, and it had been the best game she had seen all year. Her team had won 3–2 with a goal in the last minute, and she had shouted so much that her throat hurt.
Her cousin lived in Kirkby. Nadia did not. She lived in Ashwell, twenty kilometres away, and the last bus home left at half past nine.
At twenty-five past nine she was standing at the bus stop outside the stadium with four thousand other people trying to get home. At twenty to ten she was still standing there, and the bus had gone.
Nadia's first thought was to phone her mother. Then she remembered that her mother was working a night shift at the hospital and would not be able to come.
Her second thought was her phone itself, which showed four per cent battery and then, very quietly, switched itself off.
She stood still for a moment. Around her the crowd was thinning out. She counted what she had: eleven pounds, a half-eaten sandwich, and a jacket she was glad she had brought.
Then she started to walk – not towards Ashwell, which would have taken four hours, but back into the town centre, where she knew there was a café that stayed open late.

The woman behind the counter listened to the whole story without interrupting once. Then she asked Nadia if she knew her mother's number by heart. Nadia did not. She knew her own address, her cousin's street, and, for some reason, the number of her old primary school.
‘Right,' said the woman. ‘Do you know your cousin's address?'

Twenty minutes later Nadia was in a taxi that the café owner had paid for, going back to a house she had left three hours earlier. Her cousin's family had not gone to bed. They had been trying to call her since ten o'clock.

The next morning her mother came to collect her. She was not angry. On the way home she told Nadia two things: that she had done exactly the right thing by going somewhere with people and light in it, and that she was going to learn three phone numbers by heart before the week was over.
Nadia still knows them. She is twenty-four now, and she has never once needed them. She says that is not the point.

image.alt: A climber on a rock face.

listening.intro: Du kommer att höra Sara, som besöker en skola för att berätta om klättring. Berättelsen är indelad i delar. Läs frågorna först – dina svar ska vara på engelska. Du får skriva medan du lyssnar.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Hi everyone! My name is Sara Nkemelu and I work as a climbing instructor at an outdoor centre in Wales. Before that I was a maths teacher for six years. Today I'm going to tell you about the first time I ever climbed a real rock face – and about a few people who climb far better than I do.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: It happened five years ago in a valley called Llanberis, in the north of Wales. My sister had booked the trip as a present for my thirtieth birthday. I have to admit I was not very happy about it. I had never climbed anything higher than a ladder.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: We had two choices: a morning course or an afternoon one. The instructor told us to take the morning, because the rock is dry then. In the afternoon the sun moves round and the wind picks up, and wet rock is much harder to hold on to. So the morning it was.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: We were told to be at the centre at half past seven to sign in and pick up our helmets. I got there at twenty to eight. The instructor was not angry, but everyone else was already in the minibus waiting for me, and I have never been late for anything since.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: There was a family in front of me in the queue with two children. The younger one, who was nine, was not allowed to come. You have to be at least ten years old for the beginners' course, and no exceptions are made. She cried, and honestly, so did her father – he had booked it months earlier.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: The course cost forty-five pounds for adults and thirty pounds for anyone under eighteen. That included the helmet, the ropes and the instructor. You had to bring your own lunch, which I forgot.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: When we got out of the minibus the weather was perfect: sunny and quite warm, maybe eighteen degrees. Two hours later the clouds came in and it started to rain, which is very normal in that part of Wales.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: I was wearing shorts and an old pair of trainers with almost no pattern left on the bottom. What I should have brought was a jacket that keeps out rain, and proper climbing shoes with a good grip. My feet slipped three times in the first ten minutes.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: The instructor explained that the best months for climbing there are May and June. In July there are too many people, and from October the rock is often wet and cold. So if you ever go, go early in the summer.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: She also told us about the rock itself. It is called slate, and it was cut out of the mountain by workers more than a hundred years ago. That is why the walls are so straight and flat. Some of the routes still have the old workers' steps in them.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: The rule at the centre is that you never climb higher than five metres without a rope, and you always keep three points of contact – that means two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, touching the rock at all times.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Halfway up the wall the boy above me dropped his water bottle. It fell past my head and hit the ground with a bang. Nobody was hurt, but after that everyone understood why helmets are not optional.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Something similar happened in Norway two years ago, but with a much worse ending. Two climbers were on a wall when a large stone came loose above them. One of them was hit on the shoulder and could not use his arm. They were four hours from the nearest road.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: His partner had a small radio, and a helicopter came before it got dark. Both of them said afterwards that they had climbed that wall thirty times and had never once thought about what they would do if something went wrong. Now they always tell someone where they are going and when they expect to be back.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: I want to finish by telling you about a woman called Marta Reyes. She has climbed the highest mountain on each of the six continents that have them – she has not done Antarctica yet – and she is planning that one for next year.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: What I like about Marta is not the mountains. It is that she takes one young person from her old school with her on every trip, and pays for everything. Fourteen of them have gone so far. She says the mountains will still be there in a hundred years, but a fifteen-year-old only gets to be fifteen once.

listening.title: Desert Nights

image.alt: Sand dunes in the desert at sunset.

listening.intro: Du kommer att höra Amina, som besöker en skola för att berätta om sitt arbete i öknen. Berättelsen är indelad i delar. Läs frågorna först – dina svar ska vara på engelska. Du får skriva medan du lyssnar.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: Hello! My name is Amina Haddad and I work as a desert guide in southern Morocco. Before this I was a hairdresser in Marseille, in France, for eleven years. Today I'm going to tell you about my job, and about the strangest night I have ever spent in the desert.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: I take small groups out into the Sahara, usually for two or three days, with camels carrying the food and the tents. We start from a town called Merzouga, which is about ten hours by bus from Marrakesh.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: We always leave in the late afternoon, never in the middle of the day. The reason is simple: between eleven and four the sand is so hot that the camels will not walk on it, and neither will you. We walk for three hours and set up camp at sunset.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: Groups have to be at the meeting point at four o'clock. I once had a family who arrived at half past four, and we had to wait, which meant we put up the tents in the dark. Since then I tell everybody the time is half past three, and it works perfectly.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: Last spring a man wanted to bring his six-year-old daughter. I had to say no. Children under eight cannot come on the two-night trip, because it gets down to four degrees at night and there is no way back before morning. He was disappointed, but he came back in October with her on a day trip instead.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: A two-day trip costs sixty euros for adults and forty euros for children. That includes the camel, all your food and a place in a tent. What it does not include is a sleeping bag – you can rent one from us for five euros, and most people do.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: People always ask about the heat, but the thing that surprises them is the cold. In January the temperature can fall below zero at night. Even in summer you will want a jacket after midnight.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: The clothes people bring are usually wrong. You need long sleeves and long trousers, even when it is hot – they protect you from the sun far better than shorts. And you need a scarf for your head and face, which we can lend you if you don't have one.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: The best months are October, November, March and April. July and August are too hot for anyone to enjoy, and in December and January the nights are hard for people who are not used to the cold.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: The sand dunes near Merzouga are about a hundred and fifty metres high – higher than most buildings you have ever seen – and they move. A dune can travel several metres in a year, which is why the road out of town has to be cleared with a machine every spring.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: My most important rule is that nobody walks away from the camp alone at night, not even a few steps. In the dark every dune looks the same, and people have become lost forty metres from their own tent. If you need to go somewhere, you wake me up. I don't mind.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: So, the strangest night. Two years ago we were camped in a valley between two big dunes when it began to rain. It rains there perhaps twice a year. Within twenty minutes there was water running past the tents, and we had to move everything up the side of the dune at one in the morning.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: Nobody was hurt and nothing was lost, but I learned something that night: never camp at the bottom of a valley, however comfortable it looks. Now I always sleep higher up, even when the wind is worse there.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: Something much more serious happened in Algeria a few years ago. Four tourists went out without a guide and their car broke down. They had told nobody where they were going, and it took two days before anyone realised they were missing.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: They survived, but only because one of them had left a note on the table at the hotel saying which direction they planned to drive. That piece of paper was the only reason the search started in the right place.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: Finally I want to tell you about a woman called Fatima Bouzid, who has crossed the Sahara on foot three times. She is sixty-eight years old.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: What I admire is not the walking. It is that after every crossing she goes back to the villages she passed through and pays for the wells to be repaired. She says the desert has never given her anything for free, so she does not take anything from it for free either.

writing.delprov: Delprov C: writing – Food and Celebrations
writing.title: Food and Celebrations

image.alt: A table set for a meal with several dishes.

intro: En klass i Nya Zeeland arbetar med ett skolprojekt om mat och högtider i olika länder. Nu vill de veta hur det ser ut i Sverige. Läs deras brev!
Skriv så mycket du kan – och använd engelska hela tiden.
doThis: Our class is making a book about food and celebrations around the world. We have already written about our own country, and now we would like to hear from you. What do people eat where you live?

Here are some things you can write about:
• what you usually eat – on an ordinary day and on a special day
• a celebration or holiday that you like – what happens, and what you eat
• a dish you really like, or one you do not like at all – and why
• food that is typical for your area or your country
remember: Skriv på engelska hela tiden – även när du inte hittar rätt ord. Försök förklara med andra ord i stället.
Skriv så mycket du kan. Ju mer du skriver, desto mer kan du visa.
Svara på flera av punkterna i brevet, inte bara en.
Skriv som ett svar till klassen: börja och avsluta som man gör i ett brev.
Läs igenom din text när du är klar.
checklist: Jag har skrivit på engelska hela tiden.
Min text är ett svar till klassen i Nya Zeeland – den har en början och ett slut.
Jag har skrivit om flera av punkterna i brevet.
Jag har berättat om både vardagsmat och mat vid en högtid.
Jag har förklarat varför jag tycker om (eller inte tycker om) något.
Jag har använt ord och uttryck som hör ihop med mat och högtider.
Jag har läst igenom min text och rättat det jag hittade.

examples.heading: Food
paragraphs: Hello. My name is Alex. I am 12 year.
I eat pasta and pizza. I like pizza very much. On christmas we eat much food. My favorit is potatis.
I dont like fish. Bye.
comments: Texten svarar på några av punkterna: vardagsmat, en högtid och en maträtt som skribenten inte tycker om.
Den är dock mycket kort och utvecklas inte – läsaren får till exempel inte veta vad som händer på julen eller varför fisk inte är gott.
Ett svenskt ord (”potatis”) används i stället för det engelska. Nästa steg: försök förklara med andra engelska ord om du inte kommer på ordet.
Språket har fel som stör men inte förstör – en läsare med engelska som modersmål förstår ändå innehållet.

examples.heading: Food where I live
paragraphs: Hi Aroha, Tane, Mia and Josh!
Thank you for your letter. I live in a small town in the middle of Sweden and I will tell you about our food.

On a normal day we eat quite simple food. For breakfast I have yoghurt and a sandwich. At school we get a warm lunch every day, and it is free. Many people eat pancakes on Thursdays, together with pea soup. I don't know why, but we have always done it.

My favourite celebration is Midsummer in June. We put flowers on a big pole and dance around it, and then we eat outside. We have potatoes, herring, which is a small salty fish, and strawberries with cream. I love the strawberries but I really don't like the herring, because it smells so strong.
Write again and tell me what you eat in New Zealand!
Best wishes, Nora
comments: Texten är ett tydligt svar på brevet, med hälsning i början och slutet.
Flera av punkterna besvaras: vardagsmat, en högtid, en rätt hon tycker om och en hon inte tycker om.
Skribenten förklarar svåra ord för läsaren (”herring, which is a small salty fish”) i stället för att byta till svenska – det är precis vad man ska göra.
Språket flyter och är lätt att följa. Enstaka fel stör inte förståelsen.

examples.heading: Food, and what it means here
paragraphs: Dear Aroha, Tane, Mia and Josh,
Thank you for your letter – it was fun to read, and it made me think about food in a new way. I live outside Gothenburg, on the west coast of Sweden, and here food is very much about the seasons.

An ordinary weekday is not very exciting, to be honest. We eat a lot of pasta, chicken and vegetables, and the whole family eats at about six o'clock. At school we get a hot lunch every day, which I know is unusual in many countries. One day a week it is pancakes with pea soup, an old tradition that nobody can really explain any more.

The celebration I like best is Midsummer, at the end of June, when the sun hardly sets at all. We decorate a tall pole with leaves and flowers and dance around it, which probably looks very strange if you have never seen it. Afterwards we eat outdoors for hours: new potatoes with dill, several kinds of pickled herring, and strawberries with cream at the end.

If I have to choose one dish, it is my grandmother's cinnamon buns. It is not only the taste – it is that the whole house smells of them, and that she always makes far too many so that we can take some home. The one thing I cannot eat is lutfisk, a fish that is served at Christmas. It looks like jelly and I have tried twice, for my grandfather's sake.
What surprised me most about your letter was that you have summer at Christmas. Do you eat outside then? Please tell me more!
All the best, Ellinor
comments: Texten svarar på alla punkter i brevet och binder ihop dem med en egen tanke: att maten här följer årstiderna.
Innehållet är utvecklat med konkreta detaljer (”new potatoes with dill”, ”the whole house smells of them”) i stället för allmänna påståenden.
Skribenten anpassar sig till läsaren: förklarar det som kan vara okänt och avslutar med en fråga tillbaka – det gör texten till en riktig interaktion.
Språket är varierat och säkert, med både korta och längre meningar. Enstaka fel finns, men de märks knappt.

image.alt: A small town seen from above.

intro: En klass i Kanada gör en bok om platser där unga bor runt om i världen. Nu vill de veta hur det ser ut där du bor. Läs deras brev!

Here are some things you could write about:
• where you live – a town, a city or the countryside – and what it looks like
• what young people do there, and where they meet
• something you like about living there, and something you would change
• the best time of year where you live, and why
We hope to hear from you soon!
remember: Skriv på engelska hela tiden. Kommer du inte på ett ord – förklara med andra ord i stället.
Skriv så mycket du kan. Ju mer du skriver, desto mer kan du visa.
Svara på flera av punkterna i brevet, inte bara en.
Skriv som ett svar till klassen: börja och avsluta som man gör i ett brev.
Läs igenom din text när du är klar.
checklist: Jag har skrivit på engelska hela tiden.
Min text är ett svar till klassen i Kanada – den har en början och ett slut.
Jag har skrivit om flera av punkterna i brevet.
Jag har beskrivit platsen så att någon som aldrig varit där kan se den framför sig.
Jag har skrivit både något jag gillar och något jag skulle vilja ändra.

examples.heading: My town
paragraphs: Hello. I live in a small town. It is called Vara.
Here is a shop and a school. In the summer it is nice. We play football on the sportplan.
I want a bigger shop. Bye.
comments: Texten tar upp några av punkterna: var skribenten bor, vad man gör och något hen vill ändra.
Den är dock mycket kort, och läsaren får ingen bild av platsen. Vad ser man? Hur många bor där?
Ett svenskt ord (”sportplan”) används i stället för ett engelskt. Nästa steg: förklara med andra engelska ord, till exempel ”the football field”.
Språket har fel som stör men inte förstör – innehållet går att förstå.

examples.heading: Where I live
paragraphs: Hi Noor, Liam, Chloe and Deshawn!

Thanks for your letter. I live in a town called Alvesta in the south of Sweden. About eight thousand people live here, so it is not big. There is a lot of forest around us, and a lake where people swim in July.

Young people usually meet at the shopping centre or at the sports hall. On Friday evenings there is a youth club where you can play games and buy cheap food. In winter it gets dark at three o'clock, so most things happen indoors.

What I like best is that everything is close. I can walk to school in ten minutes and my friends live on the same street. What I would change is the buses. They stop at six in the evening, so if you want to do something in the bigger city you always have to ask someone's parents.
The best time of year is May, when everything turns green very quickly and it is light until late.
Write back and tell me about your town!
From Elias
comments: Texten är ett tydligt svar på brevet, med hälsning i början och slutet.
Alla fyra punkterna besvaras, och skribenten ger konkreta detaljer: åtta tusen invånare, ungdomsgården på fredagar, bussarna som slutar gå klockan sex.
Åsikterna motiveras – varför närheten är bra och varför bussarna är ett problem.
Språket flyter och är lätt att följa. Enstaka fel stör inte förståelsen.

examples.heading: A town you have never heard of
paragraphs: Dear Noor, Liam, Chloe and Deshawn,

You said you were curious about the small things, so I will start with one: the sound of my town at seven in the morning is a train. I live in Alvesta, in southern Sweden, and the railway is the reason the town exists at all. Two lines cross here, and a hundred and fifty years ago somebody decided that where they crossed, there should be a town.

About eight thousand people live here now. From above it must look like a handful of houses dropped in the middle of a forest, because that is more or less what it is. There is a lake twenty minutes away on foot, and in July it is full of children who have been waiting all year for the water to get warm enough.

Young people mostly meet in three places: outside the shop, at the sports hall, and at the youth club on Friday evenings. It is not exciting, but everybody knows everybody, which is both the best and the worst thing about living here.

That is really my answer to your third question. I like that I can walk to my friends' houses in five minutes and that nobody's parents worry when we are out. What I would change is that the buses stop running at six. If you are fifteen and you want to see a film in Växjö, you either ask an adult or you stay at home. It makes the town feel smaller than it is.
My favourite time is the two weeks in May when the birches get their leaves. It happens almost overnight, and after a long grey winter it feels like somebody has turned the colour back on.
Now tell me about your town – is it true that it snows more in Canada than here? I would like to see that.
All the best, Maja
comments: Texten svarar på alla punkter och binder ihop dem till en helhet, med en egen idé: att staden finns på grund av järnvägen.
Innehållet är utvecklat med konkreta, personliga detaljer (”the sound of my town at seven in the morning is a train”) i stället för allmänna påståenden.
Skribenten resonerar och nyanserar: att alla känner alla är både det bästa och det sämsta – det visar förmåga att se två sidor.
Texten är anpassad till läsaren: den knyter an till deras egen formulering om ”the small things” och avslutar med en fråga tillbaka.
Språket är varierat och säkert, med både korta och längre meningar.

writing.delprov: Delprov C: writing – The First Time
writing.title: The First Time

image.alt: A school newspaper team working together.

intro: Rosehill Middle School ger ut en nättidning. Nästa nummer ska handla om ett särskilt ämne – The First Time. Eleverna i redaktionen vill att du skriver en text om en gång då du gjorde något för allra första gången.
Skriv så mycket du kan – och använd engelska hela tiden.
doThis: Start with a short presentation of yourself.
There is a first time for everything. What is something you remember doing for the very first time? It does not have to be big – a first day, a first try, a first time alone.

Then choose ONE first time that you will never forget, and write about it:
– When did it happen?
– Where were you, and who was with you?
– What happened?
– How did you feel before, and how did you feel afterwards?
– Would you do it again?
Write as much as you can! Use English all the time!
remember: Skriv på engelska hela tiden. Fastnar du på ett ord – förklara med andra ord i stället.
Börja med en kort presentation av dig själv, som uppgiften ber om.
Välj en enda händelse och berätta den ordentligt, hellre än att nämna många snabbt.
Berätta både vad som hände och hur det kändes – känslorna är det tidningen är ute efter.
Läs igenom din text när du är klar.
checklist: Jag har skrivit på engelska hela tiden.
Jag har börjat med en kort presentation av mig själv.
Jag har valt en enda händelse och berättat om den.
Jag har svarat på frågorna: när, var, vem, vad som hände.
Jag har skrivit hur det kändes både före och efteråt.
Min text har en början, en mitt och ett slut.
Jag har läst igenom min text och rättat det jag hittade.

examples.heading: My first time
paragraphs: Hi. My name is Sam and I am 12. I live in Sweden.
My first time was when I ride a horse. It was scary. The horse was big and brown. I was happy after.
I want do it again.
comments: Texten följer uppgiften: en presentation och en händelse, och skribenten skriver både att det var läskigt och att det kändes bra efteråt.
Den är dock mycket kort. Läsaren får inte veta när det hände, var det var eller vem som var med – frågor som uppgiften ber om.
Verbformerna växlar (”when I ride” i stället för ”rode”). Felen stör men förstör inte förståelsen.
Nästa steg: ta en av meningarna och utveckla den med tre meningar till. Vad hände först? Vad sa någon?

examples.heading: The first time I cooked dinner
paragraphs: Hello! My name is Amina and I am twelve years old. I live in a small town in Sweden with my mum, my little brother and a very old cat.
There are many things I remember doing for the first time, like riding a bike or sleeping at a friend's house. But the one I think about most is the first time I cooked dinner alone.

It happened last autumn, on a Tuesday. My mum was working late and my brother was hungry, so I decided to make pasta with tomato sauce. Before I started I was quite nervous, because I had never used the cooker without an adult in the room.
Everything went well until I put too much salt in the water. The pasta tasted terrible. My brother ate it anyway and said it was good, which was not true, but it was kind.
Afterwards I felt proud. It was not a good dinner, but I made it myself. Now I cook once a week, and I always taste the water first. I would definitely do it again.
Amina
comments: Texten följer uppgiftens tre delar: presentation, en allmän tanke om första gånger och sedan en utvald händelse.
Alla stödfrågor besvaras – när, var, vem, vad som hände och hur det kändes före och efter.
Det finns konkreta detaljer (för mycket salt, brorsan som åt ändå) som gör berättelsen levande i stället för allmän.
Språket flyter och är lätt att följa. Enstaka fel stör inte förståelsen.

examples.heading: Twelve metres
paragraphs: My name is Oskar, I am thirteen, and until last summer I was afraid of heights. I want to tell you about the day that stopped being true.

We were at a lake outside my grandmother's village, the kind of place where nothing has changed since my mother was a child. There is a wooden tower by the water with three levels: three metres, six metres and twelve. Everybody in my family has jumped from the top. Everybody except me.

I had climbed to the twelve-metre level twice before, on two different summers, and both times I climbed back down. My cousins never said anything about it, which was somehow worse than if they had laughed.

That afternoon in July I went up again. I remember exactly how the wood felt, warm and rough under my feet, and how small the people below looked. My heart was beating so hard that I could hear it. I stood there for what my cousin later said was four minutes, but which felt like an hour.

What made me jump in the end was not courage. It was the thought of climbing down a third time and remembering it for the rest of the summer. So I stepped off the edge before I could think any more about it.

The fall lasted less than a second. Hitting the water hurt more than I expected, and I came up laughing in a way that surprised me. My grandmother, who is seventy-nine, shouted from the beach that it was about time.
I have jumped many times since then, and it is never as frightening as the first. But I am glad the first one was hard. If it had been easy, I would not still be telling you about it.
Oskar
comments: Texten gör allt uppgiften ber om, men binder ihop det till en riktig berättelse med en tydlig vändpunkt.
Känslorna visas i stället för att bara nämnas: hjärtat som bultar, träet som känns varmt och strävt, de fyra minuterna som kändes som en timme.
Skribenten reflekterar över sig själv – att det inte var mod utan tanken på att klättra ner igen som fick honom att hoppa. Det är en insikt, inte bara en händelse.
Avslutningen knyter ihop texten med en egen tanke om varför just den första gången betyder något.
Språket är varierat och säkert, med både korta och längre meningar. Enstaka fel märks knappt.
